nodes.text:
an application is made under this
section in respect of the person; or

the person gives informed consent
under this section;

It is conclusively presumed that a child who is
under 12 years of age cannot commit an
offence—see section 10 of the Youth Justice
Act 2024.
investigating official, in relation to an offence
committed outside Victoria, includes a
person (other than a person who is engaged
in covert investigations under the orders of a
superior) who is—
a member of—
the Australian Federal Police; or

the police force of another State or
a Territory; or

a person appointed by or under an Act
of the Commonwealth or another State
or a Territory whose functions or duties
include functions or duties in respect of
the prevention or investigation of
offences;

Part IC of the Crimes Act 1914 of the Commonwealth
applies if the investigating official is a member of the
Australian Federal Police.
offence includes an offence against a law of the
Commonwealth or another State or a
Territory.

An investigating official may question a person
(other than a child) who is held in a prison or
police gaol and is reasonably suspected of having
committed an offence (whether in Victoria or
elsewhere) other than the offence for which he or
she is being held about his or her involvement
(if any) in that offence if—

the investigating official is satisfied that the
person is not incapable of giving informed
consent by reason of mental impairment; and

the person gives informed consent in
accordance with subsection (13).

Section 41 of the Corrections Act 1986 provides for visits
by the police to prisoners, which may include questioning to
which this section does not apply.

A person must not be removed from the prison or
police gaol in which he or she is being held for the
purpose of questioning under subsection (11)
unless subsection (16) applies.

history.raw: S. 464B(12) inserted by No. 72/2013 s. 4(3), amended by No. 29/2020 s. 9(2).

nodes.text:
Questioning or investigations involving removal from prison
or police gaol may be authorised by a court order under
subsection (5).

A person gives informed consent to be questioned
if the person consents after an investigating
official informs the person, in language likely to
be understood by the person, of the following
matters—

the nature of the offence which the person is
suspected of having committed;
that the person may refuse to be questioned;

that if the person gives consent, he or she
does not have to say or do anything but that
anything the person does say or do may be
given in evidence;

that if the person gives consent, he or she
may withdraw that consent at any time
before the questioning is completed but
anything the person says or does before
withdrawal of consent may be given in
evidence;

that if the Magistrates' Court makes an order
under this section, the person may be
delivered into the custody of the
investigating official for the purpose of
questioning;

the person's rights under sections 464C,
464D and 464F, unless Part IC of the Crimes
Act 1914 of the Commonwealth applies.

A person may exercise any applicable right under
section 464C, 464D or 464F before deciding
whether or not to consent to be questioned.
An audiovisual recording must be made of—

the giving of the information referred to in
subsection (13); and

any response of the person in custody to the
giving of that information; and

any questioning of the person that takes
place and anything said by the person
questioned; and

any withdrawal of consent to the
questioning.

An investigating official may remove a person
being held in a police gaol for the purpose of
questioning under subsection (11) if—

the police gaol is located in the same
building as a police station; and

the person is to be removed to a room in the
police station; and

the person is not to be taken outside the
building; and

the person consents to being removed to a
room in the police station; and

the officer in charge of the police gaol gives
approval under subsection (17).

An officer in charge of a police gaol may approve
the removal of a person to a room in a police
station under subsection (16) if satisfied that the
use of the room—

is in the best interests of the person to be
questioned, having regard to privacy and
confidentiality; or

enables an audiovisual recording required by
subsection (15) to be made; or

for any other reason is preferable to
conducting the questioning in the police
gaol.

A person removed under subsection (16) from a
police gaol to a room in a police station is in the
custody of the investigating official.

The removal of a person from a police gaol to
another part of the same building under subsection

has effect as a suspension of a direction in a
warrant of commitment to deliver the person to
the place of detention specified in the warrant or
to hold the person in that place.

At the cessation of questioning, the investigating
official must deliver the person to the police gaol
from which the person was removed.

Section 78D of the Corrections Act 1986 provides for the
application of section 464B in relation to persons detained under
that Act.

nodes.heading: Right to communicate with friend, relative and legal practitioner

nodes.text:
Before any questioning or investigation under
section 464A(2) commences, an investigating
official must inform the person in custody that he
or she—
and, unless the investigating official believes on
reasonable grounds that—
the investigating official must defer the
questioning and investigation for a time that is
reasonable in the circumstances to enable the
person to make, or attempt to make, the
communication.

may communicate with or attempt to
communicate with a friend or relative to
inform that person of his or her whereabouts;
and

may communicate with or attempt to
communicate with a legal practitioner
(whether the term legal practitioner or
lawyer is used)—

the communication would result in the
escape of an accomplice or the fabrication or
destruction of evidence; or

the questioning or investigation is so urgent,
having regard to the safety of other people,
that it should not be delayed—

Subject to subsection (1), if a person wishes to
communicate with a friend, relative or legal
practitioner, the investigating official in whose
custody the person then is—

must afford the person reasonable facilities
as soon as practicable to enable the person to
do so; and

must allow the person's legal practitioner or
a clerk of the legal practitioner to
communicate with the person in custody in
circumstances in which as far as practicable
the communication will not be overheard.

This section also applies to any questioning or
investigation in accordance with an order made
under section 464B(5) or any questioning
conducted by consent under section 464B(11),
unless Part IC of the Crimes Act 1914 of the
Commonwealth applies.

This section does not apply to questioning or
investigation in connection with an offence under
section 49(1) of the Road Safety Act 1986.

If a person in custody does not have a knowledge
of the English language that is sufficient to enable
the person to understand the questioning, an
investigating official must, before any questioning
or investigation under section 464A(2)
commences, arrange for the presence of a
competent interpreter and defer the questioning or
investigation until the interpreter is present.

This section also applies to any questioning or
investigation in accordance with an order made
under section 464B(5) or any questioning
conducted by consent under section 464B(11),
unless Part IC of the Crimes Act 1914 of the
Commonwealth applies.

This section does not apply to questioning or
investigation in connection with an offence under
section 49(1) of the Road Safety Act 1986.

If a person in custody is under the age of 18 years,
an investigating official must not, subject to
subsection (2), question or carry out an
investigation under section 464A(2) unless—

a parent or guardian of the person in custody
or, if a parent or guardian is not available, an
independent person is present; and

before the commencement of any
questioning or investigation, the
investigating official has allowed the person
in custody to communicate with his or her
parent or guardian or the independent person
in circumstances in which as far as
practicable the communication will not be
overheard.

Subsection (1) does not apply if the investigating
official believes on reasonable grounds that—

the communication necessary to give effect
to subsection (1)(a) would result in the
escape of an accomplice or the fabrication or
destruction of evidence; or

the questioning or investigation is so urgent,
having regard to the safety of other people,
that it should not be delayed.

This section also applies to any questioning or
investigation in accordance with an order made
under section 464B(5).

This section does not apply to questioning or
investigation in connection with an offence under
section 49(1) of the Road Safety Act 1986.

nodes.heading: Right of foreign national to communicate with consular office

nodes.text:
If a person in custody is not a citizen or permanent
resident of Australia, the investigating official in
whose custody the person then is must, before any
questioning or investigation under
section 464A(2) commences, inform the person in
custody that he or she may communicate with or
attempt to communicate with the consular office
of the country of which the person is a citizen and,
unless the investigating official believes on
reasonable grounds that—
the investigating official must defer the
questioning or investigation for a time that is
reasonable in the circumstances to enable the
person to make, or attempt to make, the
communication.

the communication would result in the
escape of an accomplice or the fabrication or
destruction of evidence; or

the questioning or investigation is so urgent,
having regard to the safety of other people,
that it should not be delayed—

Subject to subsection (1), if a person referred to in
that subsection wishes to communicate with the
consular office of the country of which he or she
is a citizen, the investigating official in whose
custody the person then is must afford the person
reasonable facilities as soon as practicable to
enable the person to do so.

This section also applies to any questioning or
investigation in accordance with an order made
under section 464B(5) or any questioning
conducted by consent under section 464B(11),
unless Part IC of the Crimes Act 1914 of the
Commonwealth applies.

This section does not apply to questioning or
investigation in connection with an offence under
section 49(1) of the Road Safety Act 1986.

nodes.heading: Victorian Aboriginal Legal Service to be notified if Aboriginal person or Torres Strait Islander taken into custody

nodes.text: An investigating official must notify VALS if—
a person is taken into custody; and
either—

the person states (whether or not in
response to a question asked by an
investigating official) that they are an
Aboriginal person or a Torres Strait
Islander; or

the investigating official who took the
person into custody knows or is of the
opinion that the person is an Aboriginal
person or a Torres Strait Islander.

Section 464AAB requires that an investigating official
who takes a person into custody must ask the person
whether they are an Aboriginal person or a Torres
Strait Islander.
The notification must be made—

within one hour of the person being taken
into custody; or

if it is not practicable to do so within one
hour, as soon as it is practicable to do so.

As soon as practicable after VALS is notified, an
investigating official must inform the person taken
into custody of that notification.

In this section—
VALS means the Victorian Aboriginal
Legal Service Co-operative Ltd
(ABN 45 926 675 900).

nodes.heading: Recording of information required to be given to person in custody

history.raw: S. 464G inserted by No. 37/1988 s. 5, amended by No. 86/2000 s. 8(1) (ILA s. 39B(1)).

nodes.text:
If a person is in custody in relation to an
indictable offence, an investigating official who
is required by sections 464A(3), 464C(1)
and 464F(1) to give the person in custody certain
information must record (by audio recording or
audiovisual recording), if practicable, the giving
of that information and the person's responses, if
any.

Subsection (1) is subject to section 464B(5H)
and (15).

history.raw: S. 464G(2) inserted by No. 86/2000 s. 8(1), amended by No. 72/2013 s. 8.

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (2), evidence of a confession
or admission made to an investigating official by a
person who—
of having committed an offence is inadmissible as
evidence against the person in proceedings for an
indictable offence unless—
and, if either an audio recording or an audiovisual
recording was made, that recording or, if both an
audio recording and an audiovisual recording
were made, the audiovisual recording is available
to be tendered in evidence.
was suspected; or
ought reasonably to have been suspected—

if the confession or admission was made
before the commencement of questioning,
the confession or admission was recorded by
audio recording or audiovisual recording, or
the substance of the confession or admission
was confirmed by the person and the
confirmation was recorded by audio
recording or audiovisual recording; or

if the confession or admission was made
during questioning at a place where facilities
were available to conduct an interview, the
questioning and anything said by the person
questioned was recorded by audio recording
or audiovisual recording; or

if the confession or admission was made
during questioning at a place where facilities
were not available to conduct an interview,
the questioning and anything said by the
person questioned was recorded by audio
recording or audiovisual recording, or the
substance of the confession or admission was
confirmed by the person questioned and the
confirmation was recorded by audio
recording or audiovisual recording; or

if the confession or admission was made
during questioning in accordance with an
order made under section 464B(5), the
questioning and anything said by the person
was recorded by audiovisual recording—

history.raw: S. 464H(1)(f) inserted by No. 86/2000 s. 6(1)(b), amended by No. 27/2006 s. 17(6)(b).

nodes.text:
A court may admit evidence of a confession or
admission otherwise inadmissible by reason of
subsection (1) if the person seeking to adduce the
evidence satisfies the court on the balance of
probabilities that the circumstances—
are exceptional; and
justify the reception of the evidence.

If the questioning or confession or admission, or
the confirmation of a confession or admission, of
a person is recorded as required under this section
or the giving of information is recorded as
required under section 464B(5H) or 464G, the
investigating official must give to the person or
his or her legal practitioner without charge—

if either an audio recording or an audiovisual
recording was made, a copy of that recording
as soon as practicable but not later than
7 days after the recording was made; and

if both an audio recording and an audiovisual
recording were made—

the audio recording as soon as
practicable but not later than 7 days
after the recording was made; and

if the person is charged with an offence
to which the recording relates, a copy
of the audiovisual recording as soon as
practicable but not later than 7 days
after the person is charged; and

if a transcript of the recording is prepared, a
copy of the transcript as soon as practicable
but not later than 7 days after the transcript
was made.

On request by a person charged with an offence or
the legal practitioner representing that person, the
investigating official must provide an additional
copy of the audiovisual recording referred to in
subsection (3).

Nothing in this section prevents the use of an
audio recording or audiovisual recording in a
proceeding for a summary offence.

nodes.heading: No power to detain person not under arrest
nodes.text:
Nothing in sections 464 to 464H (except as
provided by an order made under section 464B(5))
confers a power to detain against his or her will a
person who is not under arrest.

history.raw: S. 464I inserted by No. 37/1988 s. 5, amended by No. 86/2000 s. 8(2).

nodes.heading: Right to remain silent etc. not affected
nodes.text: Nothing in this subdivision affects—

history.raw: S. 464J inserted by No. 37/1988 s. 5, amended by No. 84/1989 s. 6.

nodes.text:
the right of a person suspected of having
committed an offence to refuse to answer
questions or to participate in investigations
except where required to do so by or under
an Act or a Commonwealth Act; or

the onus on the prosecution to establish the
voluntariness of an admission or confession
made by a person suspected of having
committed an offence; or

the onus on the prosecution to prove that an
admission or confession was made in such
circumstances as to make it unlikely that the
truth of the admission or confession was
adversely affected; or

the discretion of a court to exclude unfairly
obtained evidence; or

the discretion of a court to exclude illegally
or improperly obtained evidence.

In this section—
authorised person means—
publish means—
recording means a recording made in accordance
with section 464B(5H), 464G or 464H.

history.raw: S. 464JA(1) def. of authorised person amended by Nos 64/2010 s. 3(1), 43/2012 s. 3(Sch. item 11.2), 82/2012 s. 159(1), 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.19(a)), 31/2024 s. 113(Sch. 1 item 7).

nodes.text:
a person or body engaged to provide
services to Victoria Police in relation to
the installation or maintenance of
recording equipment;

history.raw: S. 464JA(3)(c) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.19(b)).

nodes.text:
the Chief Crown Prosecutor or a Crown
Prosecutor or Associate Crown
Prosecutor appointed under the Public
Prosecutions Act 1994;
a legal practitioner representing—
the State; or
an informant;
a legal practitioner representing—
a co-accused of the suspect;

a court or a person acting under the
direction of a court;

the Commissioner for Law
Enforcement Data Security appointed
under Part 2 of the Commissioner for
Law Enforcement Data Security
Act 2005 or a person acting under his
or her direction;

the Chief Examiner or an Examiner
appointed under Part 3 of the Major
Crime (Investigative Powers)
Act 2004 or a person acting under the
direction of the Chief Examiner or an
Examiner;

the Commissioner within the meaning
of the Independent Broad-based
Anti-corruption Commission
Act 2011 or a person acting under his
or her direction;

the Chief Integrity Inspector within the
meaning of the Integrity Oversight
Victoria Act 2011 or a person acting
under his or her direction;

an investigating official or person
acting under his or her direction;

a person engaged by a Department or
agency to store or retrieve a record;

insert in a newspaper or other
publication; or

disseminate by broadcast, telecast or
cinematograph; or

bring to the notice of the public or any
member of the public by any other
means, including by publication on the
Internet;

A person must not knowingly possess an audio
recording or an audiovisual recording unless the
person—
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).
is the suspect; or

is a legal practitioner representing the
suspect; or

is an authorised person acting in the
performance of his or her duties; or

has possession of the recording in a sealed
package in the course of his or her duties as a
person engaged by a person referred to in
paragraph (a), (b) or (c) to transport the
recording to that person.

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 600 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

A person must not play an audio recording or an
audiovisual recording to another person unless—
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).

the recording is played for purposes
connected with any civil or criminal
proceeding and any inquiry before any court
or tribunal; or

the recording is played for purposes
connected with an investigation of a death or
a fire or an inquest held by a coroner; or

the recording is played for purposes
connected with disciplinary action against a
police officer under the Victoria Police
Act 2013; or

the recording is played for purposes
connected with disciplinary action against a
legal practitioner; or

the recording is played in accordance with
section 464JD; or

the recording is played by an authorised
person acting in the course of his or her
duties.

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 600 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

A person must not supply or offer to supply an
audio recording or an audiovisual recording to
another person other than—
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).

the suspect in relation to whom the recording
was made;
a legal practitioner representing the suspect;

an authorised person acting in the
performance of his or her duties;

a person engaged by a person referred to in
paragraph (a), (b) or (c) to transport the
recording.

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 600 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

A person, other than an authorised person acting
in the performance of his or her duties, must not
copy the whole or any part of an audio recording
or an audiovisual recording or permit another
person to make such a copy, unless the person is
acting in accordance with the direction of a court
under section 464JB.
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 600 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

An authorised person must not knowingly or
recklessly tamper with, modify or erase (in whole
or in part) a recording while the recording is being
retained under section 464JC, except in
accordance with the direction of a court under
section 464JB.
Penalty: Level 8 imprisonment (1 year
maximum).

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 600 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

A person must not publish or cause to be
published the whole or any part of an audio
recording or an audiovisual recording except in
accordance with the direction of a court under
section 464JB.
Penalty: Level 7 imprisonment (2 years
maximum).

The maximum fine that may be imposed on a body
corporate found guilty of an offence against this subsection
is 1200 penalty units: see section 113D of the Sentencing
Act 1991.

An offence against a provision of this section is a
summary offence.

nodes.heading: Court may give directions in relation to a recording

nodes.text:
In this section—
recording has the same meaning as in
section 464JA.

A court may give directions, with or without
conditions, as to the supply, copying, editing,
erasure, playing or publishing of an audio
recording or an audiovisual recording.

In this section—
authorised person has the same meaning as in
section 464JA;
court means—
Department Head has the same meaning as in the
Public Administration Act 2004;
recording has the same meaning as in
section 464JA.

history.raw: S. 464JC(1) def. of Department Head inserted by No. 64/2010 s. 4(1).

nodes.text:
if a criminal proceeding to which the
recording relates has commenced but
has not been completed, the court
hearing the proceeding;

in any other case, the Magistrates'
Court;

The Chief Commissioner of Police must keep a
copy of a recording, if the recording has been
made by a police officer in the course of an
investigation, in safe custody.

If the recording has been made by an investigating
official who is not a police officer, the recording
must be kept in the custody of the Department
Head for the Department, where the investigating
official made the recording in the course of
carrying out duties for or on behalf of that
Department.

history.raw: S. 464JC(2A) inserted by No. 64/2010 s. 4(4), amended by Nos 48/2012 s. 47, 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.20).

nodes.text:
A recording referred to in subsection (2) or (2A)
must be kept for a period of 7 years from the
making of the recording.

If the court is satisfied that there is good cause to
keep a copy of a recording for a period longer
than 7 years, the court may order that the Chief
Commissioner of Police or the Department Head
retain the copy for a further period specified in the
order.

An application for an order under subsection (3)
may be made by—

the suspect in relation to whom the recording
was made; or

an authorised person acting in the
performance of his or her duties.

The court must not make an order under
subsection (3) unless—

the court is satisfied that the applicant has
given reasonable notice of the application to
the suspect and the Chief Commissioner of
Police or the Department Head; and

the court has given the suspect and the Chief
Commissioner of Police or the Department
Head a reasonable opportunity to be heard.

nodes.heading: Use of recordings for training, teaching or testing purposes

nodes.text:
In this section—
prescribed person means—
recording has the same meaning as in
section 464JA.

history.raw: S. 464JD(1) def. of prescribed person amended by Nos 64/2010 s. 5(1), 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.21).

nodes.text:
a person or body engaged to provide
services to Victoria Police in relation to
the installation or maintenance of
recording equipment;

a legal practitioner or a person training
to become a legal practitioner;

an investigating official or a person
acting under his or her direction;

Subject to section 464JA, a recording may be
played to a prescribed person for the purposes of
training or teaching that person or testing the
recording equipment if—

the suspect has been convicted or found
guilty of the charge to which the recording
relates; and

all reasonable measures have been taken to
prevent the identification of the suspect or
any other person (including an alleged
victim) from the recording when it is played.

nodes.heading: Fingerprinting
nodes.text: Fingerprinting

nodes.heading: Fingerprinting of adults and children aged 15 or above

history.raw: S. 464K inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 25/1989 s. 11(c), 57/1989 s. 5(1)(c), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
A police officer may take, or cause to be taken by
an authorised person, the fingerprints of a person
of or above the age of 15 years who—
an indictable offence or a summary offence
referred to in Schedule 7.

history.raw: S. 464K(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.22(a)).

nodes.text:
is believed on reasonable grounds to have
committed; or
has been charged with; or

has been summonsed to answer to a charge
for—

A police officer intending to fingerprint a person
under this section must inform the person in
language likely to be understood by him or her—

history.raw: S. 464K(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.22(a)).

nodes.text:
of the purpose for which the fingerprints are
required; and

of the offence which the person is believed
to have committed or with which the person
has been charged or for which the person has
been summonsed to answer to a charge; and

that the fingerprints may be used in evidence
in court; and

that if the person refuses to give his or her
fingerprints voluntarily, a police officer may
use reasonable force to obtain them; and

history.raw: S. 464K(2)(d) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.22(a)).

nodes.text:
that if the person is not charged with a
relevant offence within 6 months or is so
charged but the charge is not proceeded with

that if the person is or has been fingerprinted
under this Subdivision on another occasion,
section 464O(3A) may apply to the
collective destruction of the person's

that the fingerprints may not be destroyed if

that the fingerprints may be used for the

the giving of that information and the person's

record (whether by audio recording or

record in writing signed by the person—

this Subdivision in relation to an indictable
offence, the giving of the information under
subsection (2) and the person's responses, if any,
must be recorded by audio recording or
audiovisual recording.

If information and a person's responses are

the recording (whether audio recording or

if a transcript of the recording is prepared, a

history.raw: S. 464K(6) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.22(b)).

A police officer may use reasonable force to take
the fingerprints of a person referred to in
subsection (1) who refuses to give them
voluntarily if the use of reasonable force is
authorised by a police officer in charge of a police

the request for the fingerprints, the giving of
the information referred to in subsection (2)
and the taking of the fingerprints; and

if the use of reasonable force has been
authorised in accordance with subsection (7),
the taking of the fingerprints must be
recorded by audiovisual recording, if
practicable, or by audio recording.

nodes.heading: Fingerprinting of children aged 14 or under

history.raw: S. 464L inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by No. 23/1991 s. 5(a)(b), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
A police officer must not do any of the following
in respect of a child who was under 12 years of
age at the time that the child is alleged to have
done any act or made any omission which would
constitute an offence if the child had been of the
age of criminal responsibility—

request the child to give the child's
fingerprints;
take fingerprints from the child;

cause any other person to take fingerprints
from the child.

It is conclusively presumed that a child who is under 12
years of age cannot commit an offence—see section 10 of
the Youth Justice Act 2024.

be requested to give his or her fingerprints;
or
have his or her fingerprints taken.

A police officer may take, or cause to be taken by
an authorised person, the fingerprints of a child
who is 12 years of age or over but under 15 years
of age and who—
an indictable offence or a summary offence
referred to in Schedule 7 if—

is believed on reasonable grounds to have
committed; or
has been charged with; or

has been summonsed to answer to a charge
for—

both the child and a parent or guardian of the
child consent; or

where consent is refused or the parent or
guardian cannot be located, the Children's
Court makes an order under
section 464M(5).

A police officer wishing to fingerprint a child
referred to in subsection (2) must inform the child
and the parent or guardian of the child in language
likely to be understood by each of them—

history.raw: S. 464L(3) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.23(a)).

nodes.text:
of the purpose for which the fingerprints are
required; and

of the offence which the child is believed to
have committed or with which the child has
been charged or for which the child has been

that the fingerprints may be used in evidence
in court; and

that the child, or the child's parent or
guardian, may refuse consent to the child's
fingerprints being taken; and

that if consent is refused, an application may
be made to the Children's Court for an order
directing the child to give the child's

that if the child is not charged with a relevant

the charge is not proceeded with or the child
is not found guilty of the offence or any

and

that if the child is or has been fingerprinted

collective destruction of the child's
fingerprints; and

that the fingerprints may not be destroyed if
the child dies before the fingerprints are
required to be destroyed; and

that the fingerprints may be used for the

A parent or guardian of a child must be present
during the request for the fingerprints under this
section, the giving of the information referred to

with consent.

Subject to subsection (6), the police officer who
informs a child of the matters in subsection (3)
must—
the giving of that information and the responses, if

history.raw: S. 464L(5) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.23(a)).

nodes.text:
record by audio recording or audiovisual
recording; or

record in writing signed by the child and the
parent or guardian present—

If a child is in custody within the meaning of this
Subdivision in relation to an indictable offence,
the giving of the information under subsection (3)
and the responses, if any, of the child and the

recording or audiovisual recording.

If information and the responses of the child and

by post to the child or the child's legal practitioner
without charge—

the recording (whether audio recording or

if a transcript of the recording is prepared, a

If information and the responses of the child and

history.raw: S. 464L(8) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.23(b)).
S. 464M inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 25/1989 s. 14(b), 57/1989 s. 5(1)(d)(e), 23/1991 s. 6(1), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
If a child referred to in section 464L(2) or the
child's parent or guardian refuses to consent to the
taking of the child's fingerprints or the parent or
guardian cannot be located, a police officer may
apply to the Children's Court for an order under
subsection (5).
An application under subsection (1)—

must be in writing supported by evidence on
oath or by affirmation or by affidavit; and

history.raw: S. 464M(2)(a) amended by No. 6/2018 s. 68(Sch. 2 item 35.3).

nodes.text:
if the child is held in a police gaol or is
detained in a youth residential centre, must
state that fact.

history.raw: S. 464M(9)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.24).

nodes.text:
Notice of an application under subsection (1) must
be served on—
a parent or guardian of the child; and

if the child is not in custody within the
meaning of this Subdivision, the child.

The court may dispense with the requirement of
subsection (3)(a) if satisfied that it is
impracticable for the applicant to comply.

The Children's Court may make an order directing
a child who is 12 years of age or over but under
15 years of age to give the child's fingerprints if
satisfied on the balance of probabilities that—

there are reasonable grounds to believe that
the child has committed an indictable
offence or a summary offence referred to in
Schedule 7; and

in all the circumstances the making of the
order is justified.

In considering whether the making of the order is
justified, the court must take into account amongst
other things—

the alleged degree of participation by the
child in the commission of the offence; and
the age of the child.

A child in respect of whom an application under
subsection (1) is made—
is not a party to the application; and

may not call or cross-examine any witnesses;
and

may not address the court, other than in
respect of any matter referred to in
subsection (5)(a) or (b) or subsection (6).

In exercising the right of address under
subsection (7)(c), a child may be represented by a
legal practitioner or, with the leave of the court, a
parent or guardian of the child.

history.raw: S. 464M(8) amended by No. 35/1996 s. 453(Sch. 1 item 16.17).

nodes.text: If the court makes an order under subsection (5)—

a parent or guardian of the child or, if a
parent or guardian cannot be located, an
independent person must be present during
the taking of the child's fingerprints; and

a police officer may use reasonable force to
take the fingerprints; and

the taking of the fingerprints must be
recorded by audiovisual recording, if
practicable, or otherwise by audio recording.
After an order under subsection (5) is executed—

the independent person, if any, who
witnessed the taking of the fingerprints must
endorse on the order the independent
person's name and sign the endorsement; and

the person who took the fingerprints must
endorse on the order the name of the person,
if any, who made the audiovisual recording
of the taking of the fingerprints; and

the person who took the fingerprints must
give a copy of the order so endorsed to the
child.

The endorsements required by subsection (10) to
be made on an order under subsection (5) may be
made on a copy of the order transmitted by
facsimile machine.

If the Children's Court makes an order under
subsection (5), it may issue a warrant authorising
the person to whom it is directed—

to break, enter and search, if necessary, any
place where the child named or described in
the warrant is suspected to be; and

to arrest the child named or described in the
warrant; and

to take the child without delay to the nearest
accessible police station for fingerprinting.

If the Children's Court makes an order under
subsection (5) or issues a warrant under
subsection (12), it must—
give reasons for its decision; and

cause a note of the reasons to be entered in
the records of the court.

The failure of the court to comply with
subsection (13) does not invalidate any order
made by it but constitutes non-compliance for the
purposes of section 464Q(1)(a).

If a child is apprehended under a warrant issued
under subsection (12), the warrant ceases to have
effect immediately after the child's fingerprints
have been taken.

If the Children's Court makes an order under
subsection (5) in respect of a child who is held in
a prison, police gaol, youth justice centre or youth
residential centre, the court must also order that
the officer in charge of the place at which the
child is held must take the fingerprints of the child
or cause them to be taken and must deliver the
fingerprints to the applicant within a period of
time specified in the order.

history.raw: S. 464M(16) amended by No. 48/2006 s. 42(Sch. item 9.3).
S. 464N inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 25/1989 ss 11(d), 12(1)(2), 14(c)(d), 56/1989 s. 286(Sch. 2 items 7.8– 7.10), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
Fingerprints may be taken by means of a device to
obtain a record of the fingerprints (a fingerscan)
or by any other means.

If—
a person of the same sex as the person to be
fingerprinted must, if practicable, take the
fingerprints and a police officer involved in
investigating the offence for which the
fingerprints are required must not, if practicable,
take the fingerprints.

fingerprints are to be taken in accordance
with a court order; or

reasonable force is to be used to take
fingerprints—

If a person of or above the age of 15 years—
a police officer may take, or cause to be taken by
an authorised person, a fingerscan of the person
for the purpose only of identifying the person.

has been charged with an indictable offence
or a summary offence referred to in
Schedule 7; and

is present in a police station because of the
charging or has been remanded in custody in
relation to the charge—

history.raw: S. 464NA(4)(b) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.25 (b)(i)).

nodes.text:
A police officer intending to fingerscan a person
under this section must inform the person, in
language likely to be understood by the person,
that the fingerscan—

is to be taken only for the purpose of
identifying the person; and
is inadmissible as evidence.

A police officer may use reasonable force to take
the fingerscan of a person referred to in
subsection (2) who refuses to allow it to be taken
voluntarily if—

history.raw: S. 464NA(4) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.25 (b)(i)).

nodes.text:
the use of reasonable force is authorised by a
police officer in charge of a police station at
the relevant time or a police officer of or
above the rank of sergeant; and

before fingerscanning the person, the police
officer informs the person, in language likely
to be understood by the person, that
reasonable force may be used to obtain it.

A person of the same sex as the person to be
fingerscanned must, if practicable, take the
fingerscan.

A fingerscan taken under this section is
inadmissible as evidence in any proceeding.

A fingerscan taken under this section which is not
required to be destroyed under section 464O may
be recorded on a computerised database and may
be accessed, disclosed, communicated or made
use of by a person for the performance of official
duties if the recording, accessing, disclosing,
communicating or making use of fingerscans on
that database by that person, or a person belonging
to a class of persons, for that purpose is authorised
in writing by the Chief Commissioner of Police.

nodes.heading: Other purposes for the use or disclosure of fingerprint information

nodes.text:
Fingerprints taken in accordance with this
Subdivision and any record, copy or photograph
of them may be used by a person authorised in
writing by the Chief Commissioner of Police for
any of the following purposes—
to identify a deceased person;

to identify a person who has suffered a
serious injury;

to identify a deceased person in a coronial
inquest or investigation.

The Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose
the identity of a person who is identified through
the use of fingerprints under subsection (1) to a
coroner.

The Chief Commissioner of Police may disclose
the identity of a person who is identified through
the use of fingerprints for the purposes of
subsection (1)(b) to a medical practitioner.

history.raw: S. 464O inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 25/1989 s. 11(e), 56/1989 s. 286(Sch. 2 items 7.11– 7.13), 57/1989 s. 5(1)(f)(i)–(iii), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
In this section—
destroy, in relation to a fingerscan, means
permanently de-identify information—
fingerprints includes fingerscan taken under
section 464NA or any other provision of this
Subdivision;
relevant offence means—

history.raw: S. 464O(1) def. of destroy inserted by No. 35/2002 s. 4.
S. 464O(1) def. of fingerprints inserted by No. 35/2002 s. 4, amended by No. 41/2004 s. 6.

nodes.text:
which identifies the person from whom
the fingerscan was taken; or

from which the person's identity may be
ascertained;

the offence in respect of which the
fingerprints were taken; or

any other offence arising out of the
same circumstances; or

any other offence in respect of which
the fingerprints have probative value.

If a person has been fingerprinted in accordance
with this Subdivision and—
the Chief Commissioner of Police must, subject to
subsections (4) and (5A), destroy the fingerprints
and any record, copy or photograph of them, or
cause them to be destroyed at the time specified in
subsection (3).

the person has not been charged with a
relevant offence at the end of the period of
6 months after the taking of the fingerprints;
or

the person has been so charged but the
charge is not proceeded with or the person is
not found guilty of the offence or any other
relevant offence, whether on appeal or
otherwise, before the end of that period—

For the purposes of subsection (2), fingerprints
taken in accordance with this Subdivision and any
record, copy or photograph of them must be
destroyed—

where the person has not been so charged or
the charge is not proceeded with, within one
month after the period referred to in
subsection (2)(a); or

where the person is not found guilty, within
one month after the conclusion of the
proceedings and the end of any appeal
period.

Despite subsection (3), if a person has been
fingerprinted in accordance with this Subdivision
on more than one occasion, those fingerprints and
each record, copy or photograph of the
fingerprints must be collectively destroyed within
one month of the date on which the person
satisfies the criteria under subsection (2) in
relation to all of those fingerprints.

history.raw: S. 464O(3A) inserted by No. 44/2022 s. 83(3), amended by No. 1/2026 s. 70(2).

nodes.text:
A police officer may, within the period referred to
in subsection (3)(a) or (b) and on one occasion
only, apply without notice to any other person to
the Magistrates' Court or the Children's Court
(as the case requires) for an order extending the
period by not more than 6 months within which
the fingerprints and any record, copy or
photograph of them must be destroyed.

history.raw: S. 464O(4) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
If a court makes an order under subsection (4), it
must cause a copy of the order to be served on the
person from whom the fingerprints were taken.

The Chief Commissioner of Police is not required
to destroy or cause to be destroyed a person's
fingerprints taken in accordance with this
Subdivision or any record, copy or photograph of
the fingerprints if—

the person has had their fingerprints taken in
accordance with this Subdivision on another
occasion and those other fingerprints are not
required to be destroyed under this section;
or

the person to whom the fingerprints belong
has died.

If fingerprints or any record, copy or photograph
of them are destroyed in accordance with this
section, the Chief Commissioner of Police must
give notice within 14 days of the destruction to the
person from whom the fingerprints were taken.

A person who—
any record, copy or photograph of fingerprints
required by this section to be destroyed is guilty of
a summary offence punishable on conviction by a
level 10 fine (10 penalty units maximum).
fails to destroy; or

uses or makes, or causes or permits to be
used or made—

history.raw: S. 464P inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by No. 25/1989 s. 11(f), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
In this section, fingerprints includes fingerscan
taken under section 464NA or any other provision
of this Subdivision.

history.raw: S. 464P(1A) inserted by No. 35/2002 s. 5, amended by No. 41/2004 s. 7.

nodes.text:
Subject to subsection (2), if—
the Chief Commissioner must without delay
destroy the fingerprints and any record, copy or
photograph of them, or cause them to be
destroyed.

a person is fingerprinted as a child in
accordance with this Subdivision, whether
before or after the commencement of
section 7 of the Crimes (Amendment)
Act 1993; and

the fingerprints are not required to be
destroyed under this Subdivision; and

in the case of fingerprints taken before the
commencement of section 7 of that Act, a
request has been made to the Chief
Commissioner of Police for their
destruction—

Subsection (1) does not apply to fingerprints
retained as a result of a finding of guilt of an
offence if—
the offence is—
an offence against this Act; or

an offence at common law the
maximum penalty for which is
specified by this Act; and

the offence is punishable by level 4
imprisonment (15 years maximum) or
more (however the penalty is described).

history.raw: S. 464Q inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 25/1989 ss 11(g)(h), 13(a)(b), 56/1989 s. 286(Sch. 2 item 7.14), 57/1989 s. 5(1)(g)(i)(ii), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
Evidence in respect of fingerprints taken from a
person is inadmissible as part of the prosecution
case in proceedings against that person for an
offence if—

the requirements of sections 464K to 464N
have not been complied with; or

the fingerprints or any record, copy or
photograph of them should have been but
have not been destroyed as required by
section 464O or 464P.

A court may admit evidence in respect of
fingerprints otherwise inadmissible by reason of
subsection (1)(a) if—

the prosecution satisfies the court on the
balance of probabilities that the
circumstances are exceptional and justify the
reception of the evidence; or

the accused consents to the reception of the
evidence.

For the purposes of subsection (2)(a), the
probative value of the fingerprints is not to be
regarded as an exceptional circumstance.

nodes.heading: Forensic procedures and DNA profile samples
nodes.text: Forensic procedures and DNA profile samples

history.raw: Heading preceding s. 464R inserted by No. 16/2002 s. 4(b), amended by No. 3/2019 s. 53.
S. 464R inserted by No. 38/1988 s. 4, amended by Nos 56/1989 s. 286(Sch. 2 item 7.15), 57/1989 s. 5(1)(h), 49/1991 s. 119(1) (Sch. 2 item 70), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
A police officer may request a suspect to undergo
a forensic procedure only if there are reasonable
grounds to believe that the procedure would tend
to confirm or disprove the involvement of the
suspect in the commission of an indictable offence
and the suspect—

history.raw: S. 464R(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
is suspected on reasonable grounds of having
committed the indictable offence; or

has been charged with the indictable offence;
or

has been summonsed to answer to a charge
for the indictable offence.

A forensic procedure may be conducted on a
suspect if—

the suspect gives his or her informed
consent; or

the Magistrates' Court makes an order under
section 464T(3) or 464V(5); or

a senior police officer gives an authorisation
under section 464SA.

history.raw: S. 464S inserted by No. 84/1989 s. 5, amended by No. 84/1989 s. 7(a)(b), substituted by No. 129/1993 s. 7.

nodes.text:
A person gives informed consent to a request to
undergo a forensic procedure if he or she consents
to the request after a police officer informs the
person in language likely to be understood by the
person—

history.raw: S. 464S(1) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
of the purpose for which the procedure is
required; and

of the nature of the procedure sought to be
conducted; and

that the person may request that the
procedure be conducted by or in the presence
of a medical practitioner or nurse or midwife
of his or her choice or, where the procedure
is the taking of a dental impression, a dentist
of his or her choice; and

of the offence which the person is suspected
of having committed or with which the
person has been charged or for which the
person has been summonsed to answer to a
charge; and

that the procedure could produce evidence to
be used in a court; and

that information obtained from analysis of
forensic material obtained by the procedure
will be placed on a DNA database and may
be used for the purpose of a criminal
investigation or any other purpose for which
the DNA database may be used under this
Subdivision or under a corresponding law of
a participating jurisdiction; and

that the person may refuse to undergo the
procedure; and

where the sample or examination sought may
be obtained by a compulsory procedure and
the person refuses to undergo the procedure,
that an application may be made to the
Magistrates' Court for an order authorising
the conduct of the procedure; and

where the sample or examination sought
may be obtained by a non-intimate
compulsory procedure within the meaning of
section 464SA and the person refuses to
consent to the procedure, that a senior police
officer may authorise the conduct of the
procedure.

A police officer who informs a person of the
matters in subsection (1)—

history.raw: S. 464S(2) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
must record the giving of the information
and the person's responses, if any, by audio
recording or audiovisual recording or in
writing signed by the person; and

must give or send by registered post to the
person or his or her legal practitioner,
without charge—

if the giving of the information and the
responses are recorded by audio
recording or audiovisual recording, a
copy of the recording as soon as
practicable, but not more than 7 days
after the information is given, and, if a
transcript of the recording is prepared, a
copy of the transcript as soon as
practicable; and

if the giving of the information and the
responses are recorded in writing
signed by the person, a copy of the
record forthwith.
A person is taken as having refused consent if—

history.raw: S. 464S(3) amended by No. 48/2006 s. 42(Sch. item 9.3), substituted by No. 3/2019 s. 54.

nodes.text: the person is—

held in a prison, police gaol or youth
justice centre; or

a prisoner in a prison or a person
detained in a police gaol who is
transferred from the prison or police
gaol to a facility or an institution
referred to in section 56AB(1) of the
Corrections Act 1986; and

within 24 hours after the giving of the
information referred to in subsection (1) the
person refuses or fails to consent to the
request to undergo a forensic procedure.

nodes.heading: Senior police officer may authorise non-intimate compulsory procedure for certain adults

nodes.text:
In this section and section 464SB, non-intimate
compulsory procedure means the taking of a
non-intimate sample or the conduct of a physical
examination of a non-intimate part of the body.

A senior police officer who is not involved in
investigating the offence for which the
compulsory procedure is required may authorise
the conduct of a non-intimate compulsory
procedure on a person if the senior police officer
is satisfied that—
the person is a relevant suspect who is—
under lawful arrest by warrant; or

in the custody of an investigating
official in accordance with an order of
the Magistrates' Court under
section 464B(5) and, at the time of the
application for that order, the person
was held in a prison or police gaol; and

the person is not under the age of 18 years;
and

the person is not incapable of giving
informed consent by reason of mental
impairment; and

the person has refused to give consent to a
request under section 464R(1); and

there are reasonable grounds to believe that
the person has committed the offence in
respect of which the authorisation is sought;
and
the requirements of section 464T(3)(c), (d),
and (f) are met; and

in all the circumstances, the giving of the
authorisation is justified.

A senior police officer must not give an
authorisation for a compulsory procedure on a
person if—

an application to a court for an order under
this Subdivision in respect of that person has
been made in relation to the same matter and
on the same grounds but has been refused; or

a previous application for an authorisation
under this section in respect of that person
has been considered in relation to the same
matter and on the same grounds but has not
been given.

An authorisation given in contravention of
subsection (3) is void.

Nothing in subsection (3) prevents a later
application for an order under this Subdivision or
an authorisation under this section on different or
further grounds.

An authorisation under this section may only be
given to a police officer.

history.raw: S. 464SA(6) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
Before a senior police officer gives or refuses to
give an authorisation under section 464SA, the
senior police officer must allow the suspect or the
suspect's legal practitioner, if any, a reasonable
opportunity, if practicable in person, to inform the
senior police officer whether there is any reason
why the non-intimate compulsory procedure
should not be conducted.

An authorisation under section 464SA must be
made in writing signed by the senior police officer
giving it and include—

the date and time when the authorisation is
given; and

history.raw: S. 464SB(6)(a) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text: the grounds for giving the authorisation; and

the type of sample or examination
authorised.

history.raw: S. 464SB(4)(c) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
The senior police officer must give, or cause
another police officer to give, to the suspect a
copy of the authorisation as soon as practicable
after the authorisation is made and, in any event,
before the conduct of the compulsory procedure.

history.raw: S. 464SB(3) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
Before the compulsory procedure is conducted, a
police officer must inform the suspect orally and
in person of the following—

history.raw: S. 464SB(4) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.text:
that an authorisation under section 464SA
has been given; and
the matters referred to in subsection (2)(a),
and (c); and

that a police officer may use reasonable force
to enable the compulsory procedure to be
conducted; and

if the authorisation is to take a sample of
hair, that the suspect may elect to provide
instead a scraping taken by the suspect from
his or her mouth, if it is considered
appropriate to do so.

The person who gives the information required to
be given by subsection (4) must—

record, or cause to be recorded, the giving of
that information by audio recording or
audiovisual recording; and

give or send by registered post, or cause to
be given or sent by registered post, to the
suspect or his or her legal practitioner,
without charge, a copy of the recording as
soon as practicable, but not more than 7 days
after the conduct of the compulsory
procedure.

If a senior police officer refuses to give an
authorisation under section 464SA in respect of a
suspect, the senior police officer must—

inform, or cause another police officer to
inform, the suspect orally of the decision as
soon as practicable after the refusal; and

give written notice of the decision to the
suspect within 7 days after the refusal.

A failure of the senior police officer or a police
officer to comply with this section does not
invalidate any authorisation made by the senior
police officer but constitutes non-compliance for
the purposes of section 464ZE(1)(a).

history.raw: S. 464SB(7) amended by No. 37/2014 s. 10(Sch. item 36.26).

nodes.heading: DNA profile sample from DNA person

nodes.text:
A police officer may request a DNA person who
is an adult to give a DNA profile sample only if
the police officer is satisfied that the taking of the
sample is justified in all of the circumstances, and
the DNA person—

is suspected on reasonable grounds of having
committed the indictable offence; or

has been charged with the indictable offence;
or

has been summonsed to answer to a charge
for the indictable offence.

A police officer may request a DNA person who
is a child to give a DNA profile sample only if the
police officer is satisfied that the taking of the
sample is justified in all of the circumstances, and
the DNA person—

is believed on reasonable grounds of having
committed the DNA sample offence; or

has been charged with the DNA sample
offence; or

has been summonsed to answer to a charge
for the DNA sample offence.
A DNA profile sample may be taken from—
a DNA person who is an adult if—
the adult gives informed consent; or
a DNA person who is a child if—

the child and a parent or guardian of the
child give informed consent; or

a senior police officer gives
an authorisation under section 464SE.

nodes.heading: Informed consent—DNA person and their parent or guardian

nodes.text:
In this section—
parent or guardian means a parent or guardian of
a DNA person who is a child.

A DNA person or a parent or guardian gives
informed consent to a request for the DNA person
to give a DNA profile sample if the DNA person
or the parent or guardian consents to the request
after a police officer informs the DNA person or
the parent or guardian in language likely to be
understood by the DNA person or the parent or
guardian—
the sample taken will be destroyed; and

of the purpose for which the sample is
required; and

of the nature of the procedure sought to be
conducted to take the sample; and

for a DNA person who is an adult, of the
indictable offence which the person is
suspected of having committed or with
which the person has been charged or for
which the person has been summonsed to
answer to a charge; and

for a DNA person who is a child, of the
DNA sample offence which the child is
believed on reasonable grounds of having
committed or with which the child has been
charged or for which the child has been
summonsed to answer to a charge; and

for a DNA person who is a child, that for the
child to give informed consent both the child
and the child's parent or guardian must
consent to the taking of the sample; and

that the taking of the sample could produce
evidence to be used in a court; and

that information obtained from analysis of
forensic material obtained by the taking of
the sample will be placed on a DNA
database and may be used for the purpose of
a criminal investigation or any other purpose
for which the DNA database may be used
under this Subdivision or under a
corresponding law of a participating
jurisdiction; and

that if a sample is taken from the DNA
person and—

the person has not been charged with an
indictable offence or a DNA sample
offence (as the case requires) at the end
of 12 months after the taking of the
sample; or

the person has been so charged but the
charge is not proceeded with or the
DNA person is not found guilty of the
offence whether on appeal or otherwise
before the end of that period—

that the DNA person or the parent or
guardian may refuse to consent to the taking
of the sample; and

that if the DNA person or the parent or
guardian refuses to consent to the taking of
the sample, that a senior police officer may
authorise the taking of the sample.

A police officer who informs a DNA person or a
parent or guardian of the matters in subsection

must record the giving of the information
and the person's responses, if any, by audio
recording or audiovisual recording or in
writing signed by the person; and

must give or send by registered post to the
person or the person's legal practitioner or
the parent or guardian of the child if the
child's legal practitioner is not known,
without charge—

if the giving of the information and the
responses are recorded by audio
recording or audiovisual recording, a
copy of the recording as soon as
practicable, but not more than 7 days
after the information is given, and, if a
transcript of the recording is prepared, a
copy of the transcript as soon as
practicable; and

if the giving of the information and the
responses are recorded in writing
signed by the person, a copy of the
record as soon as practicable.

A DNA person is taken as having refused consent
if—
the DNA person is—

held in a prison, police gaol or youth
justice centre; or

a prisoner in a prison or a person
detained in a police gaol who is
transferred from the prison or police
gaol to a facility or an institution
referred to in section 56AB(1) of the
Corrections Act 1986; and

within 24 hours after the giving of the
information referred to in subsection (2) the
DNA person fails to consent to the request to
take the sample.

A parent or guardian is taken as having refused
consent if the parent or guardian is not capable of
giving informed consent by reason of mental
impairment.

nodes.heading: Senior police officer may authorise the taking of a DNA profile sample from DNA person

nodes.text:
A senior police officer who is not involved in
investigating the offence for which the taking of a
sample is required may authorise the taking of a
DNA profile sample from a DNA person if the
senior police officer is satisfied that—
the person is a DNA person who is—
under lawful arrest by warrant; or

in the custody of an investigating
official in accordance with an order of
the Magistrates' Court or the Children's
Court (as the case requires) under
section 464B(5) and, at the time of the
application for that order, the person
was held in a prison or police gaol; and

the person is not incapable of giving
informed consent by reason of mental
impairment; and

for a DNA person who is an adult, the person
has refused to give consent to a request
under section 464SC(1); and

for a DNA person who is a child, both the
child and the child's parent or guardian have
refused to give consent to a request under
section 464SC(2); and

for a DNA person who is an adult, there are
reasonable grounds to believe the person has
committed the indictable offence in respect
of which the authorisation is sought; and

for a DNA person who is a child, the person
is believed on reasonable grounds of having
committed the DNA sample offence in
respect of which the authorisation is sought;
and

the taking of the sample without the consent
of the person is justified in all of the
circumstances.

A senior police officer must not give an
authorisation for the taking of a DNA profile
sample from a DNA person if—

an application to a court for an order under
section 464T, 464U or 464V in respect of
that person has been made in relation to the
same matter and on the same grounds but has
been refused; or

a previous application for an authorisation
under this section in respect of that person
has been considered in relation to the same
matter and on the same grounds but has not
been given.

An authorisation given in contravention of
subsection (2) is void.

Nothing in subsection (2) prevents a later
application for an order under section 464T, 464U
or 464V or an authorisation under this section on
different or further grounds.

An authorisation under this section must be given
to a police officer.

nodes.heading: Making or refusing authorisation—DNA profile sample

nodes.text:
Before a senior police officer gives or refuses to
give an authorisation under section 464SE, the
senior police officer must allow a reasonable
opportunity, if practicable in person, for the
following persons to inform the senior police
officer whether there is any reason why the DNA
profile sample should not be taken—
the DNA person;

the parent or guardian of the DNA person if
the DNA person is a child;
the DNA person's legal practitioner, if any.

An authorisation under section 464SE must be
given in writing, be signed by the senior police
officer giving it and include—

the date and time when the authorisation is
given; and
the grounds for giving the authorisation.

The Electronic Transactions (Victoria) Act 2000 applies
to enable an authorisation to be given electronically,
including facsimile transmission and email, in accordance
with that Act.

The senior police officer must give, or cause
another police officer to give, to the DNA person
a copy of the authorisation as soon as practicable
after the authorisation is made and, in any event,
before the taking of the DNA profile sample.

Before the DNA profile sample is taken, a police
officer must inform the DNA person orally and in
person of the following—

that an authorisation under section 464SE
has been given;

the matters referred to in subsection (2)(a)
and (b);

that a police officer may use reasonable force
to enable the DNA profile sample to be
taken.

The person who gives the information required to
be given by subsection (4) must—

record, or cause to be recorded, the giving of
that information by audio recording or
audiovisual recording; and

give or send by registered post, or cause to
be given or sent by registered post without

the reception of evidence otherwise inadmissible
by reason of subsection (1)(a) or (1)(ab), the court

The probative value of the evidence does not by
itself justify the reception of the evidence.

Evidence obtained as a result of a physical
examination conducted in good faith on a person
for the purposes of medical or dental treatment is
admissible in proceedings against that person for
an offence.

In this section—
child means a child who is 12 years of age or over
but under 18 years of age;
forensic sample offence means any indictable
offence or any offence specified in
Schedule 8, other than an offence heard and
determined summarily.

If a court finds a person not guilty because of
mental impairment of—
a police officer, at any time following that finding
but not later than 6 months after the final
determination of an appeal or the expiration of
any appeal period (whichever is the later), may
apply to the court for an order directing the person
to undergo a forensic procedure for the taking of a
sample from any part of the body and the court
may make an order accordingly.

a forensic sample offence (within the
meaning of that term as then in force); or

an offence of conspiracy to commit,
incitement to commit or attempting to
commit a forensic sample offence—

In an application under subsection (2), the police
officer must specify the type of sample (whether
intimate or non-intimate) sought to be taken in the
forensic procedure.
Notice of an application under subsection (2)—

must be served on the person in respect of
whom the order is sought and, if the person
is a child, on a parent or guardian of the
child; and

must include a requirement that the person in
respect of whom the order is sought attend
the hearing of the application in person or by
the person's legal practitioner.

In determining whether to make an order under
subsection (2), a court—

must take into account the seriousness of the
circumstances of the forensic sample offence
of which the person has been found not
guilty because of mental impairment; and

must be satisfied that, in all the
circumstances, the making of the order is
justified; and

may make such inquiries on oath or by
affirmation or otherwise as it considers
desirable.

An application made under subsection (2) must be
heard in the presence of the person in respect of
whom the order is sought or the person's legal
practitioner.

A person in respect of whom an application under
subsection (2) is made—
is not a party to the application; and

may not call or cross-examine any witnesses;
and

may not address the court other than in
response to inquiries made by the court
under subsection (5)(c).

In exercising the right of address under
subsection (7)(c), a person may be represented by
a legal practitioner.

An order under subsection (2) in respect of a
person who is not a forensic patient or a forensic
resident within the meaning of the Crimes
(Mental Impairment and Unfitness to be Tried)
Act 1997 must include a direction that the person
attend—
specified in the order to undergo the forensic
procedure.
at a place; and

within a period (commencing after the expiry
of the period referred to in subsection (12)
during which the order must not be
executed)—

If a court makes an order under subsection (2), it
must—

give reasons for its decision and cause a
copy of the order and reasons to be served on
the person ordered to undergo the forensic
procedure; and

inform the person ordered to undergo the
forensic procedure that a police officer may
use reasonable force to enable the procedure
to be conducted.
A failure of a court to comply with subsection

does not invalidate any order made by it but
constitutes non-compliance for the purposes of
section 464ZE(1)(a).

An order made by a court under subsection (2)
before the appeal period in relation to the verdict
of not guilty because of mental impairment has
expired or an appeal against the verdict (if any)
has been finally determined (whichever is the
later), must not be executed unless—
whichever is the later.
that appeal period expires; or
the appeal against the verdict is dismissed—

If leave to appeal against a verdict of not guilty
because of mental impairment in respect of a
forensic sample offence is sought after the expiry
of the appeal period in relation to the verdict, an
order made by a court under subsection (2) before
leave to appeal is sought, if not executed before
that leave is sought, must not be executed
unless—

leave to appeal against the verdict is refused;
or

leave to appeal against the verdict is granted
but the appeal is dismissed.

If an order made by a court under subsection (2)
has been executed after the expiry of the appeal
period in relation to the verdict of not guilty
because of mental impairment in respect of a
forensic sample offence and leave to appeal
against the verdict is granted after the expiry of
that period—

any sample and any related material and
information taken may be retained by a
police officer but may not be used for any
purpose pending the final determination of
the appeal against the verdict; and

if, on appeal, the verdict is set aside, the
Chief Commissioner of Police must, without
delay, destroy or cause to be destroyed any
sample taken and any related material and
information.

If on appeal a verdict of not guilty because of
mental impairment is set aside, an order made by
a court under subsection (2) ceases to have effect.

nodes.text:
A police officer may, at any time, direct that a
DNA profile sample be taken from a person if, at
the time that the direction is given—
the person is a registrable offender; and

the Chief Commissioner of Police does not
have a sample from the person that may be
retained indefinitely.

A senior police officer may serve, or may cause
to be served, a notice on a person referred to in
subsection (2) directing the person to attend at a
police station specified in the notice to have the
DNA profile sample taken within 28 days after
service of the notice.
A notice under subsection (3) must—

state that if the person fails to comply with
the notice, an application for a warrant to
arrest the person may be made without
further notice to the person; and

state that the person may wish to seek legal
advice as to the effect of the notice; and

state the name, rank and telephone number
of the senior police officer serving the notice
or causing the notice to be served; and
contain the prescribed information, if any.

A notice under subsection (3) must be served by
delivering a true copy of the notice to the person
personally.

Section 464ZFAA(6), (7) and (8) apply to a notice
served under subsection (3) as if it were a notice
served under that section.

If a DNA profile sample is taken from a person
under this section, the sample taken and any
related material and information may be retained
indefinitely.

Subsection (7) does not apply if, on appeal against
conviction, the finding of guilt of the registrable
offender in respect of an offence is quashed or set
aside and, but for that offence, the person would
not be a registrable offender.

Subject to subsection (10), a police officer may
give a direction under subsection (2) to a
registrable offender whose reporting obligations
under the Sex Offenders Registration
Act 2004—
only if a notice under subsection (3) has been
served on the registrable offender.
